text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
French novelist VICTOR HUGO, whose books included "LES MISERABLES", was born on this day in 1802.
"Buffalo Bill", WILLIAM FREDERICK CODY, was born in 1846. The American scout toured the US and Europe on a Wild West show from 1883, with the cast including CHIEF SITTING BULL and ANNIE OAKLEY.
SIR MUNGO McCALLUM, the Scottish professor of language and literature at Sydney University, was born in 1854.

Australian politician SIR HENRY BARWELL was born in 1877. He planned to bring British immigrant farm-labourers to South Australia to replace Australians killed in the Great War, in a scheme known as "BARWELL'S BOYS".

American actor JACKIE GLEESON was born in 1916. The singer, composer and orchestra leader made a million seller with the theme to his television series "The Honeymooners". He also made several films and was noted for his wit. He died in June 1987.

American jazz singer and pianist FATS DOMINO was born on this day in 1928. He secured a solo recording contract with Imperial Records in 1949. His first release "The Fat Man" (1950) was a million seller. PAT BOONE had a hit with FATS composition "Ain't That A Shame" (1955). Other hits for FATS included "Whole Lotta Loving" (1958), "I Want To Walk You Home" (1959) and
"Walking To New Orleans" (1960).

Country and Western legend JOHNNY CASH was born in 1932. He has had more than 110 solo hits. He began his recording career in 1955 with Sun Records. The first hits were "I Walk The Line" (1956) and "Guess Things Happen That Way" (1958). On the 14th July 1958 he switched to CBS and during the next thirty years recorded more than 1,450 tracks. His biggest pop hit was "A Boy Named Sue" (1969).
The Australian motor racing champion dubbed "Peter Perfect", PETER BROCK, was born in 1945.

British singer SANDIE SHAW (SANDRA GOODRICH) was born in 1947. Between 1964 and 69 she had eight top ten hits in the UK. These included "There's Always Something There To Remind Me" (1964) and "Puppet On A String" (1967). She was the winner of the Eurovision Song Contest in 1967.
1791 : The Bank of England issued the first ever pound
note.
1839 : The first GRAND NATIONAL steeplechase was run at
Aintree in Liverpool.
1903 : The American gunsmith who gave his name to the
multi-barrelled Gatling machine gun, RICHARD GATLING, died.
1935 : Radar was demonstrated for the first time in
England by ROBERT WATSON-WATT.
1936 : Chancellor ADOLF HITLER opened the VOLKSWAGEN
(people's car) factory in Saxony. The car was designed by FERDINAND PORSCHE, and featured a revolutionary 4-cylinder air-cooled motor.
1951 : The 22nd Amendment was passed, limiting United
States' Presidents to two four-year terms in office.
1952 : Britain announced that it had developed an Atomic
Bomb, which would be tested later in the year in the Australian desert.
1969 : Opposition Leader GOUGH WHITLAM promised a 50
million dollar emergency grant for schools if Labor was elected.
1974 : The then Prime Minister GOUGH WHITLAM came to the
defence of Aboriginal public servant CHARLES PERKINS for criticising the racial attitudes of the Liberal and Country Parties. Mr PERKINS was charged with breaching the Public
Service Act by saying in a television interview that the Opposition parties were the most racist in the world.
1980 : Egypt and Israel established diplomatic relations,
marking the end of 30 years of war between the two.
1981 : It was a meeting of "like minds" when British
Prime Minister MARGARET THATCHER met US President RONALD REAGAN for the first time in Washington.
1991 : SADDAM HUSSEIN ordered Iraqi troops out of Kuwait,
but at the same time, declared victory over the Allied Forces in OPERATION DESERT STORM.
1993 : Six people died and 1,000 others were injured when
a bomb was detonated in the World Trade Centre in Manhattan.
1995 : The London finance house of Barings collapsed
after losses run up in Singapore by trader NICK LEESON.
